preamble: The open vowel [a] (or back [ɑ]) is rounded and backed to open-mid [ɔ]. In Old English to Middle English, long ā /ɑː/ became /ɔː/ in the south and the Midlands (hām > hom, bān > bon), while Northern Middle English kept /aː/. In Bengali the Old Indo-Aryan and Prakrit inherent vowel a is pronounced [ɔ] (jala > জল /d͡ʒɔl/). In Central and Eastern Javanese, a in word-final open syllables and in an open penultimate before it became [ɔ] (Old Javanese bhāṣa > basa /bɔ.sɔ/), while Banyumasan keeps [a].

languageExamples.language: Old Javanese to Modern Javanese (Central and Eastern)

examples.note: Banyumasan and Tengger keep [apa]. Synchronically [ɔ] is the realization of /a/ in word-final open syllables and in an open penultimate before such an [ɔ] (kaya [kɔjɔ] 'like'); elsewhere /a/ stays [a] (bali [bʰali] 'to go home').

Wiktionary gives early Middle English /hɑːm/, /bɑːn/, /ɑːk/ (the Old English vowel unchanged) and Northern /haːm/, /baːn/, /aːk/, where the rounding did not take place. The new /ɔː/ was later raised to /oː/ in the Great Vowel Shift.
Middle Bengali ghor is the intermediate spelling.
The Hindi cognate सब (sab) keeps a.
